headline_marked: [[A 3.8B LLM trained to 0.384 CORE]] for just $998 in 43 hours
headline: A 3.8B LLM trained to 0.384 CORE for just $998 in 43 hours
summary: A single developer successfully trained a 3.8B parameter language model, achieving a 0.384 CORE score for under $1000. This demonstrates the growing accessibility of advanced AI model training outside of large research labs.
details: A developer successfully trained a 3.8 billion parameter Large Language Model (LLM) to a 0.384 CORE score. This impressive feat was achieved with a budget of just $998 and 43 hours of compute time, showcasing what's possible for individuals outside of major research institutions.

Inspired by Andrej Karpathy's nanochat, the project aimed to observe language emergence from scratch. The training utilized rented B200 GPUs, proving to be more cost-effective per unit of work than H100s for this specific task.

The project leveraged 'little-lm', a custom config-driven framework for training small decoder-only LLMs. This infrastructure emphasizes software engineering principles like separation of concerns and clean interfaces, allowing experiments to be expressed as simple YAML file changes.

The final model adopted a Llama-style architecture, incorporating features such as RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA (24 query heads, 8 KV heads), relu                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          to 2 MLPs, QK-norm, logit softcap, per-layer learnable residual scalars, and ResFormer-style value embeddings.

An earlier attempt to train an 858M Llama on FineWeb-Edu for 16.4B tokens over 5.8 days on a single A100 resulted in a PIQA score of 60.45%, worse than GPT-2 124M. This initial failure highlighted the need for significant optimization.

Five critical changes were implemented following the post-mortem. These included a trapezoidal learning rate schedule, the Muon optimizer for matrix parameters, switching to the ClimbMix dataset, FP8 training with vocab padding, and reducing context length to 1024.

The trapezoidal LR schedule ensured continuous learning until the end, preventing the model from coasting. Muon, while slower per step, significantly accelerated overall convergence when combined with AdamW for other parameters.

ClimbMix provided a tremendous jump in convergence speed, aligning with other research findings. FP8 training with vocab padding boosted throughput by 33%, while halving the context length effectively doubled the batch size at fixed memory, optimizing hardware utilization.

headline_marked: [[LF Edge eKuiper rewritten in Rust]] hits 425k eps, 8MB RAM, 13ms boot
headline: LF Edge eKuiper rewritten in Rust hits 425k eps, 8MB RAM, 13ms boot
summary: I-Dacs Labs has significantly boosted LF Edge eKuiper's performance for edge devices. The Rust version now processes 425,000 events/sec with minimal resources, outperforming Go eKuiper, Flink, and Benthos.
details: I-Dacs Labs has rewritten LF Edge eKuiper in Rust, achieving remarkable performance gains for edge stream processing. The new version boasts 425,000 events per second (eps), uses only 8MB of RAM, and boots in just 13 milliseconds.

This Rust rewrite significantly outperforms the original Go eKuiper, as well as Flink and Benthos, in head-to-head benchmarks. It addresses the classic resource limitations faced by high-throughput telemetry pipelines on edge devices like Raspberry Pis and embedded x86/ARM boxes.

The team utilized eKuiper for critical functions such as SQL filtering, sliding windows, and MQTT/Kafka sinks. The benchmarks involved processing a 500,000-record telemetry workload on an identical Linux machine, performing parsing, formula computation, filtering, and data projection.

All reproduction scripts and Docker configurations used for the performance testing are publicly available in a repository. This transparency allows anyone to independently verify the impressive performance metrics achieved by the Rust-based eKuiper.
